scores.evidence: Each of the 8 views has a visible one-line question as its title (e.g. 'What happens when the owner clicks Send on an email draft?'), plus a subtitle naming the audience ('Engineers onboarding to Outbound') and the scope. The level of detail (route paths, function names, bearer secrets) suits that audience.

Boxes stay at one level throughout: deployable/runtime components (UI, pages+actions, route handlers, app logic, cron, worker, volume, exit node) and external services. The views are scoped zoom-ins into the send, cron/import, refresh, scout and sign-in paths, and they share the same actors. One small conflation: 'Outbound app logic' covers both lib/engine.ts and lib/ingest.ts, but its description says 'import ingestion' and a note explains the split.

Every view shows only the actors its question needs. Omissions are stated on every view ('Not shown: Hourly Fly machine config isn't in repo; ranking math, schema columns, per-page UI'), and the scope lines point to sibling views (e.g. 'email, sourcing, sign-in and manual X sends have their own views'; 'C3–C4 … are in the machine-routes view').

Arrows are directed caller→recipient, and the legend says responses are included. Every arrow has a label saying what flows, and each label is tagged (sync) or (local), matching the solid/dotted styles. Steps are numbered A0–A7, B1–B7, C1–C4, S1–S3, L0–L2 and X1–X3, and the legend explains that 'Equal stages = alternatives; unnumbered calls are independent'. The asynchronous LinkedIn run is shown as separate POST /runs (A4) and poll (A7) calls, and the later resolution by refresh is noted.

Labelled containers separate Owner's laptop, Vercel app (managed), AWS RDS (vendor-managed), Fly threadline-browser (self-run), Fly scheduled machine, Owner home network (owner-run Tailscale exit node) and Vendor SaaS. External nodes are marked '(external)'. Trust gates (CRON_SECRET, IMPORT_TOKEN/bearer, assertOwner) appear in edge labels and notes.

Every view is a clean sequence-style layout: actors left to right, calls top to bottom, no crossings, aligned lifelines. The main text is readable at 1194x834. However, the container descriptions and the audience/scope subtitle lines render at about 9–10px, and the notes panel takes up roughly a quarter of the screen, so the secondary text is hard to read at the actual viewing size.

The visible legend on every view explains caller→recipient (response included), headers = boundaries, faint guides = actors, cylinders = stores, solid = sync request and dotted = local I/O. Line style and shape carry the meaning without relying on colour, and names match the code (sendMessage, refresh, /api/cron, /runs/{id}, browser_data, threadline-hourly-sync).

Failure behaviour and state are explicit: the conditional row claim prevents double send; in-touch lookup failure blocks the send while reply-check errors don't; limits and stage checks lead to skipped/failed; an unfinished LinkedIn run stays 'sending' after the 75s poll until refresh; runs wait for the home route with a 24h TTL; cron gets 401 without its secret, maxDuration 300s and a 230s fill deadline, and failed checks become health problems; import returns 400 on bad input; a missing worker returns 503; scraped text is untrusted and site fetches are SSRF-guarded.

The footer shows 'Source review 2026-11-05 · f467a33 + local edits · Owner: Unassigned · Live runtime NOT verified'. Names and behaviour match the code: vercel.json cron is '0 15 * * *'; cron/route.ts uses refresh({inboxWaitMs:120_000, fill:true}); sendMessage skips the limit for x_dm and uses resolveLinkedinSend(…,75_000); worker.py has QUEUE_TTL_S = 24*3600 and the /runs and /login routes. The score is capped at 3 because nothing was checked against production and two small simplifications exist (see inaccuracies).

Read in order, the views let a newcomer explain the system correctly: the owner clicks Send → server action → sendMessage claims the row → Gmail, the LinkedIn worker via the home exit node, or a hand-sent X DM. Cron and the hourly Fly machine call /api/cron → refresh, which checks replies and fills the pipeline but never sends. The scout CLI pushes to /api/import. Sign-in runs through Google OAuth and the worker's login screen proxy. The notes cover the main pitfalls.

inaccuracies: View 7 (sign-in), step S1 draws the browser going straight to Google consent. In the code, the browser first calls app/api/integrations/gmail/connect/route.ts, which checks the owner session, creates the authorization URL, sets the GMAIL_STATE_COOKIE nonce, and then redirects. That route handler hop, which creates the state the callback later checks, is missing from the drawing.

Views 1 and 4 draw the import ingestion call (C4 'ingest(FindResult)') ending at 'Outbound app logic', whose node path is lib/engine.ts. app/api/import/route.ts imports and calls ingest from lib/ingest.ts, not engine. The note text says so, but the arrow's target node is a conflation.
improvements: Make the container descriptions and the audience/scope subtitle larger (they are about 9–10px now), or shrink the notes panel, so the secondary text is readable at 1194x834.

Split 'Outbound app logic' into engine (lib/engine.ts) and ingest (lib/ingest.ts), or relabel it, so the import arrow C4 lands on the module that actually handles it. In the sign-in view, add the /api/integrations/gmail/connect redirect (where the state cookie is set) before Google consent.

Add an owner/maintainer and a production verification stamp (e.g. a confirmed Vercel cron and the Fly hourly machine schedule) to raise freshness beyond source-only review, and consider showing the refresh() resolution of 'sending' LinkedIn runs as an explicit later step in the LinkedIn view.
